1. Purpose

Assesses the drive-side harmonic currents on the Line 2 refiner feeder for EMC and power-quality compliance, and records the harmonic character of the load for reference during cable-derating checks. This sheet provides input data only; it does not itself determine the conductor size — that calculation is carried out per the cable-derating standard summary and IEC 60364-5-52.

The output is intended to support:

-   The Line 2 refiner feeder cable-sizing calculation.

-   EMC / power-quality confirmation at the Line 2 MCC busbar.

-   Cross-reference against motor-side EMC and bearing-current considerations.

2. Refiner drive input parameters

The refiner feeder design load is 45 A at 380 V (measured), matching the site supply record. The full set of drive input parameters is tabulated below:

  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Parameter                         Value                   Basis
  --------------------------------- ----------------------- ------------------------------------------------
  Drive model                       DriveTec DTX-60         Fitted frame, 30 kW nominal label

  Front-end topology                Diode bridge, 6-pulse   Standard DTX Series input stage

  Line reactor / AFE                None fitted             No active-front-end, no 12-pulse configuration

  Refiner feeder design load (Ib)   45 A at 380 V           Feeder design current, drive input side

  Nominal LV supply voltage         380 V (measured)        Site supply record
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

No line-side reactor is fitted; the harmonic spectrum below is that of a bare 6-pulse diode-bridge front-end at design duty.

3. Estimated drive input current harmonic spectrum

Typical spectrum for a 6-pulse diode-bridge VFD input at design load, without a line reactor:

  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Harmonic order (h)       Frequency (50 Hz base)   Estimated magnitude (% of fundamental)
  ------------------------ ------------------------ -----------------------------------------------
  1 (fundamental)          50 Hz                    100%

  5th                      250 Hz                   32%

  7th                      350 Hz                   16%

  11th                     550 Hz                   10%

  13th                     650 Hz                   7%

  17th, 19th, 23rd, 25th   850 Hz +                 Progressively smaller, falling roughly as 1/h
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Estimated total drive-input current THD (THDi) ≈ 38% at design duty (RMS sum of the tabulated 5th/7th/11th/13th components; higher-order terms are individually small per the 1/h trend and do not materially add to the total).

4. Spectrum character

The 6-pulse rectifier spectrum is dominated by the 5th, 7th, 11th, 13th harmonics (i.e. 6k±1 orders). It is non-triplen — the 3rd, 9th, 15th harmonics are essentially absent, as symmetrical 3-phase 6-pulse rectification does not generate significant triplen (3k) content on the line-side currents.

The spectrum is therefore characterised by:

-   Dominant orders: 5th, 7th, 11th, 13th (and higher 6k±1 members with rapidly falling magnitude).

-   Absent orders: 3rd, 9th, 15th (triplen).

-   No zero-sequence circulating current in the phase conductors from this load type.

5. Background supply distortion

Background voltage THD at the Line 2 MCC busbar, from the site supply record: ~3.5%.

This is within the compatibility level for LV industrial networks and is unchanged by the addition of the refiner drive-side spectrum above (voltage distortion at the busbar remains modest given source impedance at the 18 kA fault level).

6. Cable-derating relevance

The IEC 60364-5-52 Annex E triplen-harmonic cable derating applies only to circuits with significant 3rd/9th-order harmonic content — e.g. non-linear single-phase loads (switch-mode PSUs, discharge lighting ballasts, single-phase office loads) sharing a common neutral, where triplen currents sum in the neutral conductor and drive additional heating.

The 6-pulse drive input spectrum recorded above is non-triplen (3rd and 9th are essentially absent). Annex E does NOT apply to this feeder.

Cable current-carrying capacity for this feeder is to be verified against the IEC 60364-5-52 rating factors applicable to the as-installed conditions (grouping in adjacent drive cubicles, MCC-room ambient temperature, cable insulation class). Reference is made to the cable-derating standard summary for the applicable numeric factors.

No harmonic-based derating factor is invoked by this feeder's spectrum.

7. EMC and bearing-current implications

The drive-input harmonic content characterised above is a supply-side / line-side phenomenon. It does not, on its own, address:

-   PWM output emissions and motor-cable EMC — see IEC 61800-3 category / installation requirements and the drive dV/dt data. Motor-cable screening and 360° bonding requirements are driven by the PWM output characteristics, not by the line-side 6k±1 spectrum.

-   Bearing currents / shaft voltages — see the bearing-current application note and dV/dt data for the mitigation requirements on the motor side.

The line-side spectrum recorded here is complete for EMC / power-quality and cable-derating input purposes only; the motor-side EMC / bearing package must be assessed against the IEC 61800-3 Extract — EMC / Motor Cabling, the Drive Output dV/dt Data and the Bearing-Current / Shaft-Grounding Application Note separately.

1. Introduction
The Line 2 MDF refiner produces the wood-fibre feedstock that supplies the mat-forming station downstream. Mechanical
refining of pre-steamed chips against the disc pack is the primary energy input on Line 2, and the refiner main motor is the
single largest continuous load on the section.
Motor of record (per       Motor Nameplate Register, Line 2 refiner row):

 Item                                                            Value
 Manufacturer / model                                            Bramwell Electric Motors BEM-180L-4A
 Rated power                                                     22 kW
 Rated full-load current (FLC)                                   42 A at 400 V, 3-phase, 50 Hz
 Rated speed                                                     1465 rpm (4-pole)
 Frame / IP / insulation                                         IEC 180L / IP55 / Class F

This profile characterises the mechanical duty imposed on that motor by the refining process, so that the replacement
variable-frequency drive can be selected on the basis of duty current rather than on the motor kW label alone.

2. Duty classification
The refiner is a heavy-duty constant-torque load.
• Torque characteristic — Refining develops shear against a bed of wet chip fibre trapped between the rotating and
stationary discs. The resisting torque scales with plate gap and material presentation, not with speed. Torque demand is
present in full at any operating speed and does not fall away at reduced rpm.
• Continuous base load — Under steady refining the motor runs near full load, typically in the order of 90–95% of FLC.
There is no meaningful low-load region during production; the drive sees continuous near-rated current whenever the line is
running.
• Transient overloads — Recurring mechanical events drive the shaft torque sharply above rated:
• - *Chip-surge events* — bursts of denser or wetter feed briefly narrow the effective plate gap and load the discs.
• - *Hard-fill / plate-loading* — accumulation of compacted fibre in the refining zone before the discs clear it through.
• - *Foreign-material clearance* — tramp material (stone, metal, oversize knots) passing through the plates before ejection.
These transients are of the order of 150% of rated torque, are recurring several times per shift, and each event lasts
approximately 5 to 30 seconds before the process self-clears or the operator intervenes. They are a normal, expected
feature of refiner duty — not fault conditions.
Refiner duty is therefore in the heavy-duty (high-overload) constant-torque category. Normal-duty ratings, which assume brief
low-magnitude excursions on top of a well-below-rated continuous base, do not represent this load.

3. Implication for drive selection
Drive frames feeding this refiner must be sized on the manufacturer's heavy-duty continuous output current column, not
the normal-duty column, and not on the kW label printed on the frame.
Rationale:
1. The heavy-duty column is the current the drive can deliver continuously while retaining sufficient short-term overload
margin (typically 150% for 60 s and higher for shorter periods) to ride through recurring mechanical spikes without tripping or
derating.
2. The normal-duty column assumes the process itself limits how often and how deep the drive is called on above rated — an
assumption that does not hold for a refiner.
3. The kW label on a drive frame is a nominal marketing indicator tied to normal-duty assumptions. Matching the drive kW
label to the motor kW label understates the required drive current for constant-torque heavy-duty service.

1. Purpose
Technical characterisation of the PWM output voltage waveform produced by DriveTec DTX Series drives, presented to allow the specifying engineer to
evaluate motor-side voltage stress and specify appropriate mitigations. The values below are derived from type-test data on production DTX-45 and
DTX-60 units operating at nominal 400 V (3-phase) supply and default control settings.
2. Output waveform characteristics
 Parameter                                                                                 Value
 Applicable frames                                                                         DTX-45, DTX-60
 PWM output stage                                                                          IGBT 3-level voltage-source inverter
 Default switching frequency                                                               4 kHz (user-adjustable 2 – 8 kHz)
 Modulation                                                                                Space-vector PWM
 Typical output dV/dt (unfiltered, at drive terminals)                                     5 kV/µs
 Rise time (10 % – 90 %, unfiltered)                                                       ~100 ns
 Nominal DC-bus voltage (400 V AC supply)                                                  540 V DC
 Peak terminal voltage (motor end, with cable reflection)                                  up to ~2 × DC-bus voltage, i.e. ~1080 V, for motor-cable lengths > 20 m
 Common-mode voltage magnitude (drive output to earth)                                     ~50% of DC-bus voltage
 Common-mode dV/dt at each switching edge                                                  comparable to line-to-line dV/dt
Values are quoted for the unfiltered drive output. Reduction factors for supplementary filter options are given in §4.
3. Motor-side implications
The combination of high dV/dt (5 kV/µs) and elevated peak terminal voltage (up to ~1080 V at the motor terminals as a result of cable reflection on a 540 V
DC bus) exceeds the sinewave-only motor insulation limits defined for Category A machines (motors specified only for direct-on-line or sinusoidal-supply
operation). Where the motor connected to a DTX Series drive is not qualified for inverter duty, the following failure modes must be considered:
   • Partial-discharge (PD) activity in the turn-to-turn insulation of stator coils, driven by the steep voltage wavefront distributing non-linearly across the
   first turns of each phase winding.
   • Progressive turn-to-turn insulation failure and eventual phase-to-phase or phase-to-earth breakdown, typically presenting as a phase fault after
   weeks to months of service.
   • Bearing-current damage — capacitively-coupled shaft voltages and circulating high-frequency currents driven by the common-mode dV/dt.
   Manifests as fluting, frosting or EDM pitting on the raceways of the non-drive-end (NDE) or drive-end (DE) bearing.
The severity of each failure mode scales with switching frequency, cable length (which increases reflected peak voltage until the round-trip time exceeds
the pulse rise time), and motor age/insulation system quality.
4. Named mitigations for non-inverter-duty motors
Where the connected motor has not been qualified for inverter-duty service, one or more of the following mitigations shall be applied. Selection is the
responsibility of the specifying engineer and depends on cable length, motor age, and criticality.
   • (a) Output dV/dt filter (line-side reactor + snubber network) fitted at the drive output terminals. Reduces the effective edge rate at the motor
   terminals to below 500 V/µs and lowers the peak overshoot from cable reflection. Suitable where the primary concern is winding insulation stress and
   the motor is otherwise in serviceable condition.
   • (b) Sinewave filter (LC filter, tuned near the switching frequency) fitted at the drive output. Produces a substantially sinusoidal voltage and
   current waveform at the motor terminals, eliminating both PWM dV/dt stress and common-mode high-frequency content. Highest-cost mitigation;
   typically specified for long cable runs, retrofits with pre-1998 motors, or where multiple motors share a single drive output.
   • (c) Specify or rewind the motor to inverter-duty class, qualified per IEC 60034-18-41 (Type I, Category B or higher) for the relevant stress
   category. This is the preferred long-term solution for motors due for overhaul, and removes the requirement for output filtering.
   • (d) Fit a shaft grounding brush and/or an insulated NDE bearing to control bearing currents. A shaft grounding brush provides a low-impedance
   path from shaft to frame for capacitively-coupled shaft voltages; an insulated NDE bearing breaks the circulating-current loop through the motor frame.
   These measures address bearing damage but do not reduce winding insulation stress and are typically applied in combination with (a), (b) or (c).
5. Related references
   - IEC 60034-18-41 - Rotating electrical machines - Part 18-41: Qualification and type tests for Type I electrical insulation systems used in rotating
   electrical machines fed from voltage converters. Establishes the qualification framework and voltage stress categories referenced above (see
   reference document         in the project reference set).
   • DriveTec bearing-current application note — additional guidance on shaft-voltage measurement, bearing-current mitigation selection, and
   installation of shaft grounding hardware (project reference).
   • IEC 61800-3 — EMC requirements for adjustable-speed electrical power drive systems; specifies motor-cable screening and bonding practices that
   also influence common-mode current paths.
6. Test conditions
Values in §2 were obtained on production units under the following conditions: supply 400 V ± 1 % / 50 Hz; DC-bus at nominal 540 V; ambient 25 °C;
switching frequency 4 kHz; motor cable 30 m, screened symmetrical VFD cable, 4 × 4 mm² + concentric screen. Peak terminal voltage measured
phase-to-phase at the motor terminal box with a 100 MHz-bandwidth differential probe. Common-mode voltage measured phase-to-earth referenced to
the drive PE bar.

1. Introduction and scope
This manual covers the mechanical installation, electrical installation, EMC and grounding, safe access, insulation resistance
testing and commissioning of the DriveTec DTX Series inverter drive. The instructions apply to the two frames supplied to the
Line 2 refiner and drive cubicles at Marlden Panel Products:
• DTX-45 — nominal 22 kW frame; 45 A normal-duty / 38 A heavy-duty continuous output.
• DTX-60 — nominal 30 kW frame; 60 A normal-duty / 50 A heavy-duty continuous output.
Both frames share the same enclosure family, DC-bus topology, EMC filter, control platform and terminal layout, and are
covered by the same installation, safety and commissioning procedures. Where a paragraph applies only to one frame it is
called out explicitly.
The DriveTec DTX Series is designed and marked to the following standards:
• IEC 61800-3    - Adjustable speed electrical power drive systems - EMC requirements and specific test methods.
• IEC 61800-5-1 - Adjustable speed electrical power drive systems - Safety requirements: electrical, thermal and energy.
Compliance is conditional on installation in accordance with this manual. Departures — particularly from the motor-cable,
screen-bonding, discharge-time and IR-test instructions — will invalidate the EMC and safety declarations for the installation
and may result in equipment damage or personal injury.
This manual should be read together with the following DriveTec documents supplied for the Line 2 upgrade:

                                                                 fuses
 DTX Motor Protection Configuration Guide                        Electronic I²t motor thermal protection per IEC 61800-5-1

                                                                 time-constant, safe-access time
 DTX Commissioning Guide                                         Nameplate entry, auto-tune, parameter record procedure

Refer also to the applicable IEC 61800-3 extract in the project reference set for motor-cable screen bonding requirements
referenced from §3 and §4 of this manual.



2. Mechanical installation

2.1 Cubicle mounting

DTX-45 and DTX-60 drives are designed for wall or back-plate mounting inside a Form-3b (or better) motor control cubicle
assembled to IEC 61439-1. The drive is supplied with pre-drilled top and bottom mounting flanges. Fit all mounting bolts
specified on the general-arrangement drawing; do not omit intermediate fixings. The chassis performs both mechanical and
EMC-bonding duty (see §4).
Minimum recommended installation clearances, measured from the drive envelope to the nearest obstruction:

 Below (air inlet)                         150 mm                                     200 mm
 Side-to-side (drive to drive,             50 mm                                      75 mm
 side-vented)

 Drives may be mounted side-by-side without derating provided the side clearances above are honoured and the cubicle
ventilation section is designed to the airflow figures in §2.2.

2.2 Ventilation and cooling

The DTX Series is force-cooled by an internal top-mounted fan. Airflow requirements per drive at rated continuous output:
• DTX-45: 180 m³/h
• DTX-60: 260 m³/h
Cubicle ventilation must be sized to the sum of the installed drive flows plus an allowance for auxiliary heat sources. Filtered
inlet louvres and top-mounted extraction fans (thermostatically switched) are the recommended arrangement. Do NOT rely on
natural convection; the internal fan does not develop enough external static pressure to purge an unventilated cubicle at full
load.
The Line 2 MCC room ambient recorded at survey was above the 30 °C IEC reference ambient. This directly affects both
drive rating (see §2.3) and the ambient rating factor applied to cable sizing (refer to the project cable-sizing calculation).

2.3 Ambient limits

If the cubicle interior ambient exceeds 40 °C at full duty, size the drive up one frame or reduce the continuous load in

3. Electrical installation and cabling
CRITICAL — Read before selecting motor cable. The motor cable between the drive output terminals (U, V, W) and the
motor terminal box carries a high-dV/dt PWM waveform (typically 5 kV/µs at the drive terminals) with significant
high-frequency common-mode content. Cable selection and screen-termination on VFD output is not equivalent to
soft-starter, contactor or direct-on-line cabling practice — see §3.1 for mandatory motor-cable requirements.

3.1 Motor cable — mandatory requirements

Motor cables between the DTX drive output and the connected motor must meet all of the following:
1. Screened. The cable shall have a continuous concentric copper screen (braid, tape, or braid-plus-tape) with a coverage of
not less than 85 %. The screen provides the return path for high-frequency common-mode currents; an installation without a
continuous screen is not acceptable on the drive output under IEC 61800-3.
2. Symmetrical. The three phase conductors (U, V, W) shall be arranged symmetrically about the cable axis, with
symmetrically-disposed protective-earth conductors (typically a 3-core-plus-3-symmetrical-earth or a
3-core-plus-concentric-earth construction). Symmetrical construction cancels the low-frequency net magnetic field seen
outside the cable and equalises the earth-return impedance between the three phases.
3. Rated for PWM inverter output. The cable insulation shall be rated for the peak terminal voltage produced by
cable-reflection at the motor terminals (up to approximately twice the DC-bus voltage) and for the elevated dielectric stress
imposed by PWM switching. Cables marked to VDE 0250, HD 604, or an equivalent inverter-output rating are acceptable.
Constructions specifically marked inverter-duty, VFD cable, or PWM-rated satisfy all three requirements simultaneously and
are the recommended default.
An unscreened cable of the type used for legacy soft-starter or DOL feeds does not satisfy any of the three requirements
above and shall not be installed on the drive output.

3.2 Screen termination
 The cable screen shall be terminated with a low-impedance 360° connection at both ends of the run — at the drive/MCC
end into the drive gland plate, and at the motor end into the motor terminal-box gland plate. The 360° termination is achieved
using an EMC gland (also known as an EMC cable gland or screened gland) which grips the exposed cable screen
circumferentially and bonds it directly to the metallic gland plate.
The requirement for both-end screen bonding on VFD motor cables is set by IEC 61800-3 and is repeated in the referenced
project extract. The screen termination at each end must provide a defined low-impedance path over the switching-frequency
band of the drive output.
Refer to the EMC gland manufacturer's datasheet supplied with the project (Kelbrook Cable Components KCC-EMC Series
or equivalent approved product) for the correct gland size against cable overall diameter, and for the stripping/preparation
dimensions. Fit the gland strictly to the datasheet — an over-stripped or under-stripped screen will not clamp correctly and will
not achieve a 360° bond.

3.4 Coordinating fuses (input side)

The DTX Series achieves its conditional short-circuit rating of 65 kA only when the specified aR (semiconductor) coordinating

Only the aR (fully-rated for semiconductor protection) family is acceptable. gG general-purpose or standard MCB coordination

3.5 Cable run lengths

Motor cable length between drive and motor should be kept as short as practical. For runs longer than 30 m consult DriveTec
regarding fitting an output dV/dt filter or output choke — the cable-reflection peak at the motor terminals rises with run length
and can exceed the motor insulation rating on runs of several tens of metres.



4. EMC and grounding

4.1 Grounding hierarchy

Grounding on a DTX installation serves three distinct functions and must not be conflated:
1. Protective earth (PE) — safety earth to IEC 61800-5-1. Sized to at least the phase-conductor cross-section; landed on the
drive PE stud with a dedicated cable lug.
2. Signal / control-cable screen earth — bonded at one end (typically the drive/control-panel end) for control and
instrumentation screens to avoid low-frequency earth loops on analogue signals. This convention applies to control wiring
only.
3. Motor-cable screen EMC bond — bonded at both ends via a 360° EMC gland, as set out in §3.2 and IEC 61800-3.
The three functions coexist. The motor-cable screen bonding requirement is set by IEC 61800-3 and is applied at both cable
ends per §3.2 of this manual.

4.2 EMC gland — hardware
 Refer to the EMC gland datasheet supplied with the project reference set (Kelbrook KCC-EMC Series or approved
equivalent) for:
• gland body size against cable outer diameter,
• inner and outer seal ring selection,
• screen-cutback dimension (typically 15 ± 2 mm),
• installation torque on the gland body and the entry thread,
• the metallic gland plate preparation (unpainted, clean, corrosion-protected).
Do not select the gland by phase-conductor size alone; the seat that grips the screen is dimensioned to the cable overall
diameter, not the copper. A gland fitted to the wrong overall diameter will not close 360° on the screen and will not achieve
compliance with IEC 61800-3.

4.3 IEC 61800-3 — where to look

The relevant clause on motor-cable screen bonding in IEC 61800-3 is included in the project reference set. Read that extract
in conjunction with §3.2 of this manual and the EMC gland datasheet before signing off the cable terminations.

4.4 Cabinet bonding

Bond the drive chassis to the cubicle back-plate through the mounting studs — the back-plate itself is part of the EMC
reference. Use a serrated-washer stack under each mounting bolt to bite through paint and achieve a metal-to-metal bond, or
specify an unpainted mounting zone. Bond the gland plate to the back-plate through the same construction. Verify continuity
between the drive chassis, gland plate and cubicle earth bar with a milli-ohmmeter after installation.



5. Safety — stored energy (DC bus)


   CAUTION - DC-BUS STORED ENERGY

   The DTX Series contains DC-bus capacitors that retain hazardous charge after the AC supply is isolated.
   Upstream isolation alone is not sufficient to make the drive-side terminals safe.

   Wait a minimum of 8 minutes after supply isolation and verify by measurement that the DC-bus voltage has
   decayed to less than 50 V before accessing any drive-side terminal, opening the enclosure, or disconnecting the
   motor cable.

   Prove dead with a suitable voltage indicator on all live parts, including DC+ / DC-, U/V/W and the input terminals
   L1/L2/L3, before any work commences.




5.1 Why 8 minutes

The DTX-45 and DTX-60 DC-bus is designed with an internal bleed resistor that discharges the capacitor bank from the
nominal 540 V bus voltage through a first-order RC decay. With the specified bank capacitance and bleed-resistor
values (see the DC-bus discharge data sheet), the time to decay below 50 V is approximately 8 minutes.
The 8-minute figure is the manufacturer-stated safe-access time and applies to all DTX-45 and DTX-60 units regardless of
loading history. Do not rely on unaided estimation or shortcut wait times such as "a minute or two after the contactor drops
out" — the RC decay is exponential and the bus can hold well above 50 V for several minutes after the AC supply is removed.

5.2 Prove-dead

After the 8-minute wait, and before any contact with drive-side terminals:
1. Confirm the upstream isolation is in place and locked off (LOTO).
2. Apply a calibrated non-contact or contact voltage indicator across DC+ / DC− and confirm < 50 V.
3. Repeat across U–V, V–W, U–W and each phase to PE, confirming < 50 V on each pair.
4. Prove the indicator on a known live source before and after the measurement (three-point test).
5. Record the discharge-verification time and reading on the isolation log / permit-to-work.
The upstream isolation and the discharge verification are two separate steps. Both are required before drive-side work;
neither can substitute for the other.

5.3 Additional safety notes
 • Do not defeat the DC-bus discharge circuit or shortcut the wait time with an external discharge resistor of unspecified rating
— an external discharge without knowledge of the bank energy can generate an arc-flash hazard.
• Do not connect or disconnect the motor cable with the drive energised.
• Do not run the drive with the enclosure door open other than under a specifically drafted commissioning permit; some
measurement points are exposed at hazardous voltages during running.
• The DTX Series is designed to IEC 61800-5-1 for basic and supplementary insulation; PE integrity is a mandatory protective
measure and must be verified at commissioning.



6. Insulation resistance (IR) testing

6.1 Isolate the drive output before applying test voltage

Insulation resistance testing of the motor and motor cable is required before energisation and periodically thereafter. IR
testing applies a DC test voltage (typically 500 V or 1000 V DC) that is incompatible with the drive output stage. Applying
an IR test through the drive will damage the drive electronics.
Always isolate the drive output before applying an IR test voltage to the motor circuit. Isolation means physically
disconnecting the U, V, W conductors from the drive output terminals — a control-side stop or a run-inhibit input is not
sufficient.

6.2 Test procedure

1. Confirm the drive is off, isolated upstream and locked off.
2. Confirm the 8-minute DC-bus discharge time has elapsed and the bus has been verified below 50 V (see §5).
3. Disconnect the motor cable conductors U, V, W (and any brake resistor, DB+/DB−, if fitted) from the drive terminals.
Insulate the loose ends.
4. Apply the IR test voltage between each motor circuit conductor and PE, and between each pair of phase conductors, at the
motor terminal box or at the disconnected drive-end lugs.
5. Record IR readings and temperature.
6. Re-terminate at the drive; torque to §3.3; record.

6.3 If in doubt

If there is any uncertainty as to whether the drive output has been isolated from the circuit under test, stop and confirm before
applying voltage. IR damage to the output stage is not covered by warranty.



7. Commissioning overview
The DTX Series ships with a generic factory template configuration. The factory template is not a commissioned
configuration and must not be treated as ready-to-run. Commissioning requires per-motor parameterisation from the
connected motor's nameplate, plus a drive auto-tune, plus an update of the site drive-parameter record.
Follow the DTX Commissioning Guide (the VFD Parameter & Commissioning Guide) in full. In outline:
1. Enter motor nameplate values (kW, voltage, rated current, frequency, rated speed, cos φ, connection) from the motor rating
plate — not from a kW-derived assumption and not from the factory template.
2. Select the drive duty class (Normal Duty / Heavy Duty) to match the driven-load duty category. Refer to §5 of the datasheet
       and the load duty profile.
3. Run the drive auto-tune (stationary or rotating, per the VFD Parameter & Commissioning Guide) to identify stator
resistance, leakage inductance and magnetising current for the connected motor.
4. Configure the electronic motor thermal protection (I²t) parameters — rated current, thermal time constant, overload class,
cooling method — from the motor nameplate, following the DTX Motor Protection Configuration Guide .
5. Set application-level parameters (ramp times, current limits, PID loops, digital and analogue I/O assignments) per the drive
parameter record.
6. Update the drive parameter record and have it counter-signed before running the motor under load.
Do not attempt production start-up on the factory template. The template's motor parameters are generic and will
misconfigure both the flux control and the electronic thermal protection for the connected motor.

KCC-EMC Series Cable Glands

Datasheet KCC-DS-EMC-2025


1. Overview
The KCC-EMC Series comprises nickel-plated brass cable glands intended for the termination of screened power and control
cables at metallic gland plates and motor terminal boxes. The EMC variants provide a 360° low-impedance contact between
the cable screen and the gland plate, and are the correct termination for the motor cable of a Variable Frequency Drive (VFD).
The Standard variants (pigtail tail) are supplied for applications in which a single-end screen earth is required, typically
instrumentation and low-level signal circuits where the screen carries no continuous common-mode current.
All glands in this datasheet are manufactured from CZ121 brass with a nickel plating finish; ingress protection is IP68 (mated)
with the appropriate O-ring and seal. Threads are metric parallel (ISO 262/965), suitable for direct entry into a threaded gland
plate or via a locknut on a clearance hole.

3. EMC data
The 360° EMC contact provides a low-impedance high-frequency screen termination essential for EMC compliance.
High-frequency screen currents require a low-impedance 360° termination to be effective.
The spring-finger contact ring inside the KCC-EMC body engages the exposed braid of the cable screen and clamps it
uniformly around the full circumference against the gland body, which is bonded to the gland plate through the thread and
locknut. Measured transfer impedance of the KCC-EMC-25 termination is less than 5 mΩ at 30 MHz on braid-screened
symmetrical VFD cable, tested to the internal method KCC-TM-04.
By contrast, a pigtail tail — in which the braid is gathered into a short length of conductor to a nearby earth stud — introduces
series inductance of the order of 1 µH per 25 mm of tail. At the switching-edge frequencies produced by a modern PWM
inverter (in the range of several MHz), the resulting impedance is orders of magnitude higher than a 360° termination. A
pigtail tail is therefore not equivalent to a 360° EMC gland for the purposes of terminating a VFD motor cable, even where the
DC continuity of the screen is otherwise identical.
 A screened symmetrical VFD motor cable is intended to be terminated with a 360° EMC gland at the gland plate on which the
cable lands. The 360° gland provides the low-impedance screen path required by IEC 61800-3.

4. Note
This datasheet provides hardware options only. The correct choice for a given cable installation must be worked out against
the applicable EMC requirement (see IEC 61800-3).

1. Introduction
Every DriveTec DTX Series drive leaves the factory pre-loaded with a generic factory template parameter set. The template
is provided so the drive powers up, communicates over the keypad and fieldbus, and can be bench-tested by the panel
builder or site electrician before the motor is present. It is not matched to any specific motor.
The template motor block carries nominal placeholder values selected to keep the drive in a safe internal state on the bench;
those placeholder values are printed on the drive's commissioning label and appear in the parameter record file supplied with
each unit. They are deliberately generic and have no relationship to the motor the drive will eventually control.
Before the drive is used to run a motor on load — even for a bump test, a rotation check, or a low-speed jog — the factory
template must be replaced with commissioned per-motor values taken from that specific motor's nameplate, and an
auto-tune must be completed for the drive/motor pair. This applies to every drive on the installation, including drives supplied
as spares that are later swapped into service.
The remainder of this guide sets out the five-step commissioning sequence that DriveTec requires for each DTX drive on site.
The sequence is short but each step is mandatory.



2. Step 1 — Read the motor nameplate
Locate the driven motor and read its nameplate. Record the following values on the site drive parameter record before
touching the drive keypad:
• Rated voltage (V) — the voltage stamped on the nameplate for the connection configuration in use (star or delta). Where the
nameplate shows dual voltages, record the value matching the actual terminal-box connection.
• Rated current (A) — the full-load current at the recorded rated voltage.
• Rated frequency (Hz) — 50 Hz or 60 Hz as stamped.
• Number of poles — 2, 4, 6, 8… Where the nameplate does not list poles explicitly, derive from the rated speed and
frequency.
• Rated speed (rpm) — the full-load speed at rated frequency, not the synchronous speed.
• Full-load power factor (cos φ).
• Rated shaft power (kW).
If any nameplate field is illegible or missing, do not guess and do not substitute values from a similar motor. Stop and obtain
the motor manufacturer's data sheet or type-test certificate before proceeding.
Notes on older motors. Where the plate does not stamp cos φ or rated speed, use the motor manufacturer's data sheet for
that exact type and serial range. A generic estimate is not acceptable — the auto-tune in Step 3 depends on accurate starting
values.
Site rules. All nameplate readings must be witnessed by a second person and logged with date and initials on the site drive
parameter record. This is the audit trail that the drive's motor thermal model was configured from data specific to the
connected motor.



3. Step 2 — Enter per-motor nameplate values into P1.xx
Enter the recorded values into drive parameter group P1.xx (Motor Data) via the keypad or DriveTec commissioning tool:

 P1.01                                      Motor rated shaft power (kW)               Nameplate
 P1.02                                      Motor rated current (A)                    Nameplate
 P1.03                                      Motor rated voltage (V)                    Nameplate (connection matched)
 P1.04                                      Motor rated frequency (Hz)                 Nameplate
 P1.05                                      Number of poles                            Nameplate / derived
  P1.06                                      Motor rated speed (rpm)                   Nameplate
 P1.07                                      Rated cos φ                               Nameplate

Overwrite the template placeholder values entry-by-entry. Do not import a saved parameter file from another drive/motor pair
as a shortcut — the P1.xx block is per-motor, and importing another motor's block replaces one incorrect template with
another.
After entry, read back each P1.xx value on the keypad and verify against the site record before moving on. The drive's
electronic thermal protection (I²t model, per IEC 61800-5-1) is derived from P1.02 in particular — an incorrect value here
means the drive's overload protection is protecting the wrong motor.



4. Step 3 — Run auto-tune
With the P1.xx block correctly populated, initiate an auto-tune from parameter P1.20 (Auto-tune mode):
• Stationary auto-tune (P1.20 = 1) — the drive injects test currents with the shaft at rest. Suitable where the motor is coupled
to the load and cannot rotate freely, or where uncoupling is not practical. Measures stator resistance and leakage inductance;
estimates magnetising inductance from nameplate data.
• Rotating auto-tune (P1.20 = 2) — the drive spins the motor uncoupled at reduced flux. Required where high dynamic
performance, low-speed torque, or sensorless vector control is needed. Measures stator resistance, leakage inductance, and
magnetising inductance directly, and identifies the rotor time constant.
Choose the mode appropriate to the drive/motor/load configuration. For refiner, extruder, conveyor, and other constant-torque
loads on the DTX-60 in heavy-duty configuration, rotating auto-tune is recommended where the mechanical arrangement
permits safe uncoupled rotation; otherwise use stationary.
Auto-tune must be completed for each drive/motor pair. A tune performed on one drive/motor combination is not
transferable to another drive, even of the same frame size and firmware level, because the measured stator resistance and
leakage inductance are unique to the physical cable-length, terminations, and motor-winding condition of that specific pair.
On completion the drive writes the measured values into parameter group P1.30–P1.39 (Motor Model). Confirm the tune
completed without fault code (F.201 through F.209 indicate a failed tune — see the DTX Installation & Operating
Manual) and record the resulting stator resistance, leakage inductance, and magnetising inductance on the site drive
parameter record.



5. Step 4 — Set application parameters
With the motor model established, configure the application-level parameters for the driven load:
• Ramp times (P2.01 acceleration, P2.02 deceleration) — set to values consistent with the driven inertia and any
process-side constraints. Default 5 s ramps (P2.01/P2.02 as shipped) are rarely correct for high-inertia or constant-torque
loads.
• Torque limits (P3.10 motoring, P3.11 regenerating) — set the motoring limit to the drive/motor combination's continuous
heavy-duty capability, expressed as % of motor rated torque. Set the regenerating limit consistent with any braking-resistor or

· Overload class (P3.20) - select the IEC 60947-4-1 overload class matching the driven load: Class 10 for standard duty,
Class 20 or Class 30 for heavy-duty starting profiles. Confirm the selected class against the process engineer's duty
specification.

compensation causes low-speed overheating; insufficient compensation causes stall at start.
Where the drive is fed via a coordinating fuse (aR type) for conditional Icc, verify that the fuse fitted upstream matches the
type specified in the DTX Series Datasheet for the frame in question. The conditional Icc rating only applies with the specified
fuse in place.



6. Step 5 — Record the as-set parameters
On completion of Steps 1–4, transcribe every P1.xx and application parameter, together with the auto-tune results, into the
site drive parameter record. The record must be kept per drive/motor pair, dated, signed by the commissioning engineer,
and countersigned by the site's responsible electrical engineer.
The as-set record is the reference used for:
• Post-commissioning parameter integrity checks (compare live drive values against the record).
• Drive-swap events (a replacement drive must be commissioned from the record's P1.xx entries and re-tuned — the record is
the source of nameplate data, the tune is not carried over).
• Statutory and third-party inspection.
Until the as-set record is completed and signed, the drive/motor pair is not commissioned regardless of whether the motor
has turned.
 7. Cautions
Do NOT run the motor on the shipped template — template values are generic placeholder values and are not
matched to any specific motor. Running a motor on template values risks overload trips, incorrect thermal
protection, poor torque control, and (for oversized template) unprotected motor windings.
• The template's rated current is used by the drive's electronic thermal protection. If the template current is higher than the
connected motor's rated current, the motor can be overloaded well beyond its thermal capability before the drive trips — the
winding can reach damaging temperatures with no fault indication at the drive.
• The template's rated voltage, frequency, poles, and cos φ are used by the drive's V/f and vector control loops. Incorrect
values produce poor torque response, oscillation at low speed, and audible acoustic noise at the motor.
• Auto-tune values (stator resistance, leakage inductance, magnetising inductance) are measured per drive/motor pair. Reuse
of another pair's values, or use of the template's placeholder motor-model values, will result in the drive's control loop being
tuned to a motor that is not the one connected.
If in doubt at any step, stop and contact DriveTec Systems technical support before proceeding.

Manufacturer application note | Doc DTX-AN-BC-2025-01 | DTX Series inverter drives (all frames)

Business Park, Warwick CV34 6RB

7032 44 8812
Issue: 2025-01 · Supersedes: nil


1. Phenomenon
PWM voltage-source inverters generate a common-mode voltage across the motor windings that couples
capacitively to the rotor shaft. If not mitigated, the resulting shaft voltage discharges through the bearing races
via Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) currents, pitting the raceways and eroding the bearing grease — a
failure mode absent on sinusoidal supply.
The mechanism is intrinsic to PWM inverter operation: the summed instantaneous phase-to-neutral voltage at
the motor terminals is non-zero and switches at the drive's carrier frequency (nominally 4 kHz on the DTX
Series). This common-mode voltage divides across the parasitic capacitances of the motor — stator winding to
frame, stator winding to rotor, and rotor to frame through the bearing lubricant film. When the film breaks down,
the accumulated shaft charge discharges as a high-frequency EDM pulse through the ball-to-race contact.

2. Symptoms
The mode is progressive and typically presents in service as:
- Audible bearing noise (a rising "growl" or intermittent whine) developing over weeks to months after
  commissioning on the VFD.
- On removal and inspection, fluting or washboarding of the bearing race - characteristic evenly-spaced
  ridges running circumferentially around the raceway - accompanied by darkened, degraded grease.
- Premature bearing failure typically at 6 to 18 months, on motors that gave no bearing trouble under prior
  soft-starter or direct-on-line operation.
Symptoms usually appear first at the non-drive end (NDE), because the drive-end bearing is more often earthed
via the driven load.

3. Applicable Motors
The failure mode is most severe on:
- Motors not qualified for inverter duty - i.e. no shaft-grounding brush and no insulated NDE bearing fitted
  from the factory - that are reused on VFD supply. Refer to the IEC 60034-18-41 extract for the
  inverter-duty qualification criteria.
- Larger frames (broadly, motors above 10 kW), where the greater shaft area increases capacitive coupling.
- Installations with longer motor cables (typically above 20 m), which raise the peak terminal voltage through
  transmission-line reflection and increase common-mode current.
- Drives with high dV/dt output. The dV/dt data sheet records the DTX Series unfiltered output at
  approximately 5 kV/us; the steeper the edge, the greater the high-frequency common-mode content.
Inverter-duty motors supplied on new installations are ordinarily specified with these mitigations from the factory
and are not the target of this note.

4. Mitigation Options
The mitigations below can be applied singly or in combination. In descending order of typical field priority for
retrofit:




                DriveTec App Note DTX-AN-BC-2025-01 — Bearing Currents & Shaft Grounding | Page 1
 (a) Shaft grounding brush. A carbon-fibre or micro-fibre shaft grounding ring is fitted concentric to the motor
shaft, ordinarily at the NDE, providing a low-impedance shaft-to-frame bond that shunts the induced shaft
voltage to earth before it can discharge through the bearing. Retrofit rings are available as split-ring designs that
can be installed without dismantling the shaft.

(b) Insulated NDE bearing. A ceramic hybrid bearing (steel races with ceramic rolling elements) or a
fully-insulated outer-race bearing at the NDE breaks the electrical path from rotor to frame through that bearing.
This forces any remaining shaft current to seek an alternative return, which — combined with a shaft grounding
brush — is diverted safely to earth.

(c) Output dV/dt filter. A drive-mounted dV/dt filter (or sinusoidal output filter for the most demanding cases)
reduces the magnitude and edge rate of the common-mode voltage at the motor terminals, lowering the shaft
voltage that develops across the parasitic capacitance divider.

(d) Common-mode choke. A three-phase common-mode choke fitted on the drive output attenuates the
high-frequency common-mode current at source. Complements the above; particularly useful where multiple
motors share a drive line-up and cabling.

5. Recommendation — Reused Motors
For reused non-inverter-duty motors, fit a shaft grounding brush at minimum; consider an insulated NDE bearing
in addition for critical-duty motors (continuous operation, high shaft speed, extended cable runs, or restricted
maintenance access). Where the motor is being fed from a DTX drive at default switching frequency and no
output filter is fitted, both measures are advised for any motor above 10 kW that will run more than intermittently.

The suitability of a specific motor for reuse on a DTX drive should be confirmed against the inverter-duty
insulation qualification in IEC 60034-18-41 in parallel with the bearing-current assessment
above. Insulation stress and bearing stress are separate failure modes and each must be addressed.

Extract from IEC 61439-1 & IEC 60947-2 — Low-voltage switchgear and controlgear assemblies / Circuit-breakers
Version 2024-01
Reference sheet prepared by Marlden Engineering. Plain-language summary for internal design and verification use. Not a
substitute for the full published IEC text — consult the current issue of IEC 61439-1 and IEC 60947-2 for authoritative
wording.



1. Assembly short-circuit withstand
The assembly (MCC/DB) shall be marked with either an Icw (rated short-time withstand current) or an Icc (conditional
short-circuit rating) that is at least equal to the prospective fault current at its point of installation.
Where the assembly rating is expressed as an Icc, the marking is only meaningful in combination with the upstream
short-circuit protective device (SCPD) specified by the assembly manufacturer under IEC 61439-1. Where the rating is
expressed as an Icw, the assembly is capable of withstanding the stated current for the associated short-time duration without
reliance on a specified upstream device.
For device-level ratings inside the assembly, IEC 60947-2 defines the corresponding ratings for circuit-breakers (Icu —
ultimate short-circuit breaking capacity; Ics — service short-circuit breaking capacity). Where a circuit-breaker or drive is
offered with a conditional Icc, the same principle applies: the rating is qualified by the specified coordinating device fitted
upstream.

2. Conditional short-circuit rating (Icc)
Where a device or assembly is marked with a CONDITIONAL Icc, that rating is VALID ONLY when the specified upstream
coordinating device (typically an aR semiconductor fuse) is fitted upstream. Absent the specified coordinating device, the
device/assembly is only rated to its standalone short-circuit rating, which is typically much lower.
The conditional Icc is a coordination rating between the downstream device and a named upstream protective device —
commonly an aR (semiconductor / drive-protection) fuse of a particular manufacturer, rating and characteristic. The rating
relies on the aR fuse operating fast enough to limit the let-through I²t and peak current to values the downstream device can
survive. Substituting a different fuse type (for example a gG utilisation-category fuse), a fuse of the wrong rating, or a
moulded-case circuit-breaker in place of the specified aR fuse invalidates the conditional Icc.
The headline conditional Icc figure quoted on a device datasheet is therefore not a self-contained compliance statement. It
represents the rating that applies when — and only when — the coordinating device named on the same line of the datasheet
is present upstream.

3. Verification
Before energising, verify:
(a) the prospective fault current at the point of installation (from fault-level study);
(b) the standalone and conditional ratings of the device from its datasheet;
(c) that the specified coordinating device is actually fitted upstream (from the as-built device list).
Each of the three verification steps is independent. A satisfactory fault-level study alone does not establish compliance; nor
does a datasheet quotation of a conditional Icc without the corresponding as-built confirmation that the named coordinating
device has been installed in the correct feeder position with the correct rating and characteristic. All three records —
fault-level study, device datasheet, as-built device list — should be filed together in the pre-energisation verification pack.

4. Failure mode
Fitting a device with only a standalone rating below the prospective fault current risks catastrophic device failure under fault.
Where the standalone rating of the fitted device is below the prospective fault current and the specified coordinating device is
absent, incorrectly rated, or of a non-equivalent type, the device is not capable of interrupting or withstanding the available
fault energy. The failure mode is not limited to the tripping of the affected circuit: fault energy in excess of the device's
withstand can produce arcing, ejection of hot gas and molten conductor material, mechanical destruction of the cubicle
interior, and consequential damage to adjacent equipment and personnel in front of the panel.
Assembly designations under IEC 61439-1 (arc-fault behaviour, form of separation) do not compensate for a mis-rated
device. A device operated above its actual (unconditional) short-circuit rating will fail regardless of the assembly's form of
separation.

Extract from IEC 61800-5-1: Adjustable Speed Electrical Power Drive Systems — Part 5-1: Safety requirements —
Electrical, thermal and energy — Version 2024-02
Reference: MPP-STD-SUM-07 | Prepared: Marlden Engineering



Principle
Power drive systems present stored-energy and thermal hazards that require specific safety provisions beyond conventional
switchgear practice. IEC 61800-5-1 sets out the electrical, thermal and stored-energy safety requirements applicable to
adjustable-speed power drive systems (PDS): protection against electric shock from live parts and residual voltages,
protection against thermal hazards, and the safety provisions relied upon for motor overload protection when the drive itself
performs that function. Panel practice for direct-on-line and soft-starter installations does not translate directly to PDS; the
additional hazards (DC-bus stored energy, PWM-fed motor thermal behaviour) must be addressed on the terms set by this
standard and by the manufacturer's data for the specific drive.



Key provisions
• Stored energy — DC-bus. DC-bus capacitors retain charge after supply isolation. The standard requires that access to the
drive is not authorised until the manufacturer-stated discharge time has elapsed AND the DC-bus has been proven dead with
an approved instrument at the drive DC-bus terminals. Verification is made at the drive terminals themselves — not upstream
of the drive, and not from a downstream indicator.
• Isolation and stored energy. Locking off the incoming supply removes the source but does not remove the energy already
stored on the DC bus. Isolation is applied together with the discharge-wait interval specified by the drive manufacturer and
with a prove-dead measurement at the drive DC-bus terminals in accordance with the sequence recorded on the site
permit-to-work and isolation procedure.
• Motor overload protection. IEC 61800-5-1 permits the drive's integrated electronic thermal protection (I²t model,
configured from motor rated data — rated current, service factor, cooling method) to fulfil the motor-overload protection
function of the powered branch circuit. Where this protection is correctly configured from the motor nameplate, an additional
series thermal overload relay in the motor branch circuit is not required.
• Applicable discharge time. The applicable DC-bus discharge time for a specific drive frame is the value stated by the drive
manufacturer in the drive documentation. That value is the interval to observe on site; it is the discharge interval to be
recorded on the isolation log and referenced on any permit-to-work covering drive-cubicle access.
• Sequence of access. The general sequence to be followed on any drive cubicle is: isolate at the upstream isolator and
apply lock-off / tag; wait the manufacturer-stated discharge time from the drive documentation; prove dead at the DC-bus
terminals with an approved, in-date instrument, using a known-live proving source before and after; record the discharge time
and prove-dead result on the isolation log entry before authorising work.

Extract from IEC 60034-18-41 — Rotating Electrical Machines: Qualification of Type I Insulation Systems
for Inverter-Driven Machines
Marlden Panel Products — Standards Library | MPP-STD-LIB-034-18-41 | IEC 60034-18-41 Version 2014-03
Held by Engineering Records (D. Okonkwo) — Site copy: Marlden Works, Dumfries
Controlled reference sheet. Consult the full published IEC 60034-18-41:2014 for authoritative text.
1. Principle
Motors fed from PWM voltage-source inverters are subjected to high-frequency dV/dt and repetitive impulse voltages that are not present on a sinusoidal
supply. Each switching event of the drive output stage produces a steep-fronted voltage transient which, when propagated along the motor cable, is
amplified at the motor terminals by transmission-line reflection. The resulting peak line-to-line voltage at the winding, together with its rise-time, is the
governing electrical stress on the turn-to-turn and phase-to-phase insulation.
A motor whose insulation system was designed for 50 Hz sine-wave operation is not, by that fact alone, qualified for inverter supply. Insulation systems
used on inverter-driven machines must be qualified explicitly against the PWM stress regime defined in IEC 60034-18-41.
2. Scope — Type I insulation systems
The standard applies to Type I insulation systems: random-wound stator windings of the kind used in low-voltage industrial induction motors (typically ≤
700 V rated line-to-line). Type I systems are not designed to operate with sustained partial discharge activity; qualification therefore aims to demonstrate
that, under the specified inverter stress, partial discharge inception is not exceeded during the declared service life.
Qualification requires testing against defined impulse-voltage and dV/dt limits, expressed per stress category determined by the motor rated voltage
class in combination with the drive dV/dt and connecting cable length:
 • Category A — benign stress (short cables, moderate dV/dt); the least onerous impulse envelope.
 • Category B — moderate stress; intermediate impulse envelope.
 • Category C — enhanced stress (long cables and/or high dV/dt drives); the most onerous envelope, corresponding to the highest peak terminal
   voltages and shortest rise-times.
An insulation system qualified for one category is not automatically qualified for a more onerous one. The category is set by the actual installed conditions
— drive output dV/dt, cable length, and rated voltage — not by the motor alone.
3. Motors predating the standard or not qualified
Motors not qualified per IEC 60034-18-41 — including all motors manufactured before the first edition was in general application (typically pre-2014) and
motors whose nameplate carries no inverter-duty declaration — may fail prematurely under PWM stress even if healthy on a sine-wave supply. The
two dominant electrical failure modes observed in the field are:
 • Partial discharge erosion of turn insulation. Repetitive PWM impulses drive local field concentrations at the first few turns of each coil above the
   partial discharge inception voltage; discharge activity erodes the enamel over hundreds to thousands of hours, culminating in a turn-to-turn short.
 • Motor termination failures. The reflected peak at the motor terminals stresses the phase-to-phase insulation at the connection block and the first
   turns of each phase, producing tracking, flashover, or line-to-line breakdown at the terminals.
Neither failure mode is detectable by routine IR (insulation resistance) testing prior to occurrence — a passing IR test on an older motor does not
demonstrate inverter-duty suitability.
4. Screening question for reuse
Before feeding an existing motor from a new inverter, confirm each of the following. Any negative answer requires replacement, rewind to inverter-duty
specification, or the mitigation options in §5.
 • Nameplate marking. Is the motor labelled as inverter-duty qualified? Look for an explicit statement (e.g. "inverter-duty", "VPI inverter-duty class",
    "suitable for PWM inverter supply", IE-class efficiency marking combined with an inverter qualification declaration, or a reference to IEC 60034-18-41
    stress category).
 • Installation / manufacture year. Motors installed or manufactured before approximately 2014 are typically not qualified. Absence of an inverter-duty
    statement on a pre-2014 nameplate should be treated as "not qualified" unless positive evidence to the contrary is on file.
 • Cable length between drive and motor. Long motor cables amplify the reflected terminal voltage; the longer the cable, the higher the stress
    category required. Record actual installed cable length and compare to the drive dV/dt data sheet when placing the installation in Category A / B
    / C.
5. Mitigation options for motors NOT inverter-duty qualified
Where the screening question in §4 concludes that a motor is not qualified, the following mitigations are available. Selection depends on cable length,
drive output characteristics, motor condition, and remaining service life required.
 • Retrofit a dV/dt output filter at the drive output terminals. Limits the rate-of-rise of the output waveform, reducing both the reflected peak amplitude
   and the frequency content that drives partial discharge activity in the winding.
 • Retrofit a sinewave (LC) filter at the drive output. Reconstructs a near-sinusoidal waveform at the motor terminals, effectively removing PWM stress
   from the winding. Larger, heavier and more costly than a dV/dt filter; may require de-rating of the drive.
 • Motor rewind to inverter-duty specification — rewind with an insulation                    ified per IEC 60034-18-41 to the appropriate category, together
   with any bearing-current mitigation identified from the associated app-note.
The mitigation route chosen should be recorded against the motor in the nameplate register and reflected in the drive commissioning parameters.
6. Related references
 •         DriveTec DTX Series drive output dV/dt data; peak-terminal-voltage and rise-time figures used to place the installation in Category A / B / C.

1. Purpose and Scope
This procedure defines the site standard for safe isolation of electrical plant prior to inspection, testing, maintenance,
modification, or any other work where the presence of energy at the point of work could injure the person carrying out that
work or a person nearby.
The procedure is issued under the authority of the Health & Safety / Compliance Manager and applies to:
• All Marlden Panel Products employees engaged in electrical work of any description on any Marlden site.
• All contractors, sub-contractors, vendor engineers, and visiting specialists working on Marlden electrical plant, whether
under a site permit or under a supervised task instruction.
• All voltage classes present on site, from the 11 kV incomer down to auxiliary and control circuits.
• All three production lines (Line 1, Line 2, Line 3) and the associated MCCs, distribution boards, and field-mounted
equipment.
The procedure sets out the minimum controls that must be in place before an item of plant is treated as safe for access.
Where a task-specific method statement imposes stricter controls, the stricter control takes precedence. This document is not
to be departed from without prior written concession from the Health & Safety / Compliance Manager.
Where installed equipment falls into a category for which a supplementary addendum exists (see Addendum A, VFD
Stored-Energy Addendum, at the end of this document), the main body procedure is to be followed and the addendum
applied in addition. No addendum reduces the controls in the main body.



2. Definitions
For the purposes of this procedure, the following terms carry the meaning set out below.
Isolation. The disconnection and separation of an item of plant from every source of electrical supply, in such a manner that
the disconnection is secure and cannot be re-made without the deliberate act of a competent person.
Point of isolation. The physical device — normally an upstream circuit-breaker, isolator, or fused switch — at which the
supply to the item of plant is broken. The point of isolation must be capable of accepting a lock and a tag.
Lock-off. The application of a personal padlock to the point of isolation such that the device cannot be operated back into the
closed position without removal of the lock. Each individual carrying out work under the isolation shall fit their own personal
lock; multi-lock hasps shall be used where more than one person is working under the same isolation.
Tag (caution tag). A durable label attached at the point of isolation identifying the person who has fitted the lock, the date
and time of isolation, the work being carried out, and the isolation log reference (ISO-####).
Prove-dead (proving-dead). The act of verifying, at the load-side terminals of the isolation or at the point of work, that no
dangerous voltage is present between phases and between each phase and earth. Proving-dead is carried out using an
approved voltage-proving device that has itself been proven on a known live source, or against a proving unit, immediately
before and immediately after the dead check.
Approved voltage-proving device. A two-pole voltage indicator conforming to GS38 and to IEC 61243-3, drawn from the
calibrated test-gear register held by Maintenance Stores. Multimeters are not approved for proving-dead.
Competent person. A person who, by reason of training, qualification, and experience, is authorised in writing by the Chief
Electrical Engineer to carry out the class of electrical work in question. The authorisation is recorded on the personnel
competence register held by HSE.
Isolation log. The site register (ISO-#### numbered) in which every isolation carried out under this procedure is recorded.
The isolation log is a legal record and shall be completed contemporaneously.



3. General LOTO Procedure
The general procedure set out in this section shall be followed for every electrical isolation carried out on site. The steps are
given in the order in which they shall be performed and shall not be re-ordered.

from docx import Document
from docx.shared import Pt, Cm, RGBColor
from docx.enum.text import WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH, WD_BREAK
from docx.enum.table import WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT, WD_CELL_VERTICAL_ALIGNMENT
from docx.enum.section import WD_ORIENT
from docx.oxml.ns import qn
from docx.oxml import OxmlElement
import re

NAVY = RGBColor(0x1F, 0x38, 0x64)
GREY = RGBColor(0x55, 0x55, 0x55)
HDR_FILL = "1F3864"
SUB_FILL = "D9E2F3"
CALL_FILL = "F2F2F2"


def new_document():
    doc = Document()
    sec = doc.sections[0]
    sec.page_width = Cm(21.0)
    sec.page_height = Cm(29.7)
    sec.left_margin = Cm(2.0)
    sec.right_margin = Cm(2.0)
    sec.top_margin = Cm(1.8)
    sec.bottom_margin = Cm(1.7)
    sec.header_distance = Cm(0.8)
    sec.footer_distance = Cm(0.8)

    st = doc.styles["Normal"]
    st.font.name = "Calibri"
    st.element.rPr.rFonts.set(qn("w:eastAsia"), "Calibri")
    st.font.size = Pt(10)
    st.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(4)
    st.paragraph_format.line_spacing = 1.08

    for name, size, before, after in [("Heading 1", 14, 12, 6), ("Heading 2", 11.5, 10, 4), ("Heading 3", 10.5, 8, 3)]:
        h = doc.styles[name]
        h.font.name = "Calibri"
        h.element.rPr.rFonts.set(qn("w:eastAsia"), "Calibri")
        h.font.size = Pt(size)
        h.font.bold = True
        h.font.color.rgb = NAVY
        h.paragraph_format.space_before = Pt(before)
        h.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(after)
        h.paragraph_format.keep_with_next = True

    lb = doc.styles["List Bullet"]
    lb.font.name = "Calibri"
    lb.font.size = Pt(10)
    lb.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(2)
    return doc


def _add_field(run, instr):
    f1 = OxmlElement("w:fldChar"); f1.set(qn("w:fldCharType"), "begin")
    it = OxmlElement("w:instrText"); it.set(qn("xml:space"), "preserve"); it.text = instr
    f2 = OxmlElement("w:fldChar"); f2.set(qn("w:fldCharType"), "end")
    run._r.append(f1); run._r.append(it); run._r.append(f2)


def header_footer(doc, left_text, right_text, footer_text):
    sec = doc.sections[0]
    hp = sec.header.paragraphs[0]
    hp.text = ""
    r = hp.add_run(left_text); r.font.size = Pt(8); r.font.color.rgb = GREY
    hp.add_run("\t\t")
    r2 = hp.add_run(right_text); r2.font.size = Pt(8); r2.font.color.rgb = GREY
    _bottom_border(hp)

    fp = sec.footer.paragraphs[0]
    fp.text = ""
    r = fp.add_run(footer_text + "    Page "); r.font.size = Pt(8); r.font.color.rgb = GREY
    r = fp.add_run(); r.font.size = Pt(8); r.font.color.rgb = GREY; _add_field(r, "PAGE")
    r = fp.add_run(" of "); r.font.size = Pt(8); r.font.color.rgb = GREY
    r = fp.add_run(); r.font.size = Pt(8); r.font.color.rgb = GREY; _add_field(r, "NUMPAGES")
    fp.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.RIGHT


def _bottom_border(p):
    pPr = p._p.get_or_add_pPr()
    pbdr = OxmlElement("w:pBdr")
    b = OxmlElement("w:bottom")
    b.set(qn("w:val"), "single"); b.set(qn("w:sz"), "4"); b.set(qn("w:space"), "1"); b.set(qn("w:color"), "999999")
    pbdr.append(b); pPr.append(pbdr)


TOKEN = re.compile(r"(\*\*.+?\*\*|__.+?__)")


def rich(p, text, size=None, color=None, bold=False, italic=False):
    """Add text to paragraph p, honouring **bold** and __italic__ markers."""
    for part in TOKEN.split(text):
        if not part:
            continue
        b, i = bold, italic
        if part.startswith("**") and part.endswith("**"):
            part = part[2:-2]; b = True
        elif part.startswith("__") and part.endswith("__"):
            part = part[2:-2]; i = True
        run = p.add_run(part)
        run.bold = b
        run.italic = i
        if size:
            run.font.size = Pt(size)
        if color:
            run.font.color.rgb = color
    return p


def para(doc, text, size=None, bold=False, italic=False, after=None, before=None, align=None, color=None, keep=False, indent=None):
    p = doc.add_paragraph()
    rich(p, text, size=size, bold=bold, italic=italic, color=color)
    pf = p.paragraph_format
    if after is not None:
        pf.space_after = Pt(after)
    if before is not None:
        pf.space_before = Pt(before)
    if align:
        p.alignment = align
    if keep:
        pf.keep_with_next = True
    if indent is not None:
        pf.left_indent = Cm(indent)
    return p


def bullet(doc, text, size=None, level=0):
    p = doc.add_paragraph(style="List Bullet")
    rich(p, text, size=size)
    if level:
        p.paragraph_format.left_indent = Cm(0.63 + 0.6 * level)
    return p


def numbered(doc, n, text, size=None, hang=0.6):
    p = doc.add_paragraph()
    pf = p.paragraph_format
    pf.left_indent = Cm(hang)
    pf.first_line_indent = Cm(-hang)
    pf.space_after = Pt(3)
    pf.tab_stops.add_tab_stop(Cm(hang))
    rich(p, f"{n}\t" + text, size=size)
    return p


def shade(cell, fill):
    tcPr = cell._tc.get_or_add_tcPr()
    shd = OxmlElement("w:shd")
    shd.set(qn("w:val"), "clear"); shd.set(qn("w:color"), "auto"); shd.set(qn("w:fill"), fill)
    tcPr.append(shd)


def cell_margins(table, top=50, bottom=50, left=80, right=80):
    tblPr = table._tbl.tblPr
    mar = OxmlElement("w:tblCellMar")
    for k, v in (("top", top), ("left", left), ("bottom", bottom), ("right", right)):
        e = OxmlElement(f"w:{k}"); e.set(qn("w:w"), str(v)); e.set(qn("w:type"), "dxa"); mar.append(e)
    tblPr.append(mar)


def fixed_layout(table):
    tblPr = table._tbl.tblPr
    lay = OxmlElement("w:tblLayout"); lay.set(qn("w:type"), "fixed"); tblPr.append(lay)


def repeat_header(row):
    trPr = row._tr.get_or_add_trPr()
    h = OxmlElement("w:tblHeader"); h.set(qn("w:val"), "true"); trPr.append(h)


def no_split(row):
    trPr = row._tr.get_or_add_trPr()
    c = OxmlElement("w:cantSplit"); c.set(qn("w:val"), "true"); trPr.append(c)


def fill_cell(cell, text, size=8.5, bold=False, color=None, align=None):
    cell.text = ""
    lines = text.split("\n") if isinstance(text, str) else [str(text)]
    first = True
    for line in lines:
        p = cell.paragraphs[0] if first else cell.add_paragraph()
        first = False
        p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(1)
        p.paragraph_format.space_before = Pt(0)
        p.paragraph_format.line_spacing = 1.0
        if line.startswith("• "):
            p.paragraph_format.left_indent = Cm(0.3)
            p.paragraph_format.first_line_indent = Cm(-0.3)
        rich(p, line, size=size, bold=bold, color=color)
        if align:
            p.alignment = align
    cell.vertical_alignment = WD_CELL_VERTICAL_ALIGNMENT.TOP


def table(doc, headers, rows, widths, size=8.5, header_size=8.5, header_fill=HDR_FILL, zebra=False, first_col_bold=False, cant_split=True):
    t = doc.add_table(rows=1, cols=len(headers))
    t.style = "Table Grid"
    t.alignment = WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT.CENTER
    t.autofit = False
    fixed_layout(t)
    cell_margins(t)
    hdr = t.rows[0]
    repeat_header(hdr)
    for i, h in enumerate(headers):
        c = hdr.cells[i]
        fill_cell(c, h, size=header_size, bold=True, color=RGBColor(0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF))
        shade(c, header_fill)
    for ri, r in enumerate(rows):
        row = t.add_row()
        if cant_split:
            no_split(row)
        for i, val in enumerate(r):
            c = row.cells[i]
            fill_cell(c, val, size=size, bold=(first_col_bold and i == 0))
            if zebra and ri % 2 == 1:
                shade(c, "F7F9FC")
    for row in t.rows:
        for i, w in enumerate(widths):
            row.cells[i].width = Cm(w)
    # spacing after table
    doc.add_paragraph().paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(2)
    return t


def kv_table(doc, pairs, widths=(4.0, 13.0), size=9, key_fill=SUB_FILL):
    t = doc.add_table(rows=0, cols=2)
    t.style = "Table Grid"
    t.alignment = WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT.CENTER
    t.autofit = False
    fixed_layout(t)
    cell_margins(t)
    for k, v in pairs:
        row = t.add_row()
        no_split(row)
        fill_cell(row.cells[0], k, size=size, bold=True)
        shade(row.cells[0], key_fill)
        fill_cell(row.cells[1], v, size=size)
    for row in t.rows:

1 Reconciliation — drawing by drawing

1.1 The test applied

Three references decide each call.

-   Restart Criterion 3 (MPP-RC-L2-001 Rev A, §4). The controlled record set must match the as-installed condition of Line 2 before verification proceeds. Each approved RFI affecting a drawing is either incorporated at re-issue or presented with the still-issued drawing and its field markup, as QMS-STD-ENG-001 §5 requires. Every open RFI affecting Line 2 is closed before the verifier's visit. Superseded drawings are not relied on.

-   QMS-STD-ENG-001 Rev D, §3–§5. Every field change to an issued drawing needs a numbered, approved RFI. A field markup is red pen on a print of the current issued revision. A re-issue takes the next revision letter and cites the RFIs it incorporates. A revision letter is never used twice. Title-block status is one of four values: ISSUED FOR CONSTRUCTION, FOR APPROVAL, AS-BUILT or SUPERSEDED.

-   The Line 2 RFI register (Engineering/RFIs/Line2_RFI_log.xlsx, last updated 07/14/2026) is what each drawing answers to. The as-installed condition is taken from the isolation log, the IR test record (07/25/2026), the Drive Parameter Record, P. Nandwani's termination notes (07/11/2026) and the refiner drive export (08/06/2026).

Standards cited in this document: IEC 61800-3 — Adjustable speed electrical power drive systems — Part 3: EMC requirements and specific test methods; IEC 60364-5-52 — Low-voltage electrical installations — Part 5-52: Selection and erection of electrical equipment — Wiring systems; IEC 61439-1 — Low-voltage switchgear and controlgear assemblies — Part 1: General rules; IEC 60947-2 — Low-voltage switchgear and controlgear — Part 2: Circuit-breakers. Short forms are used after this point.

-   Unverified by its own account. Rev B describes itself as “updated per RFI-014; other rows carried forward from pre-upgrade schedule pending verification”. On its own statement it is not an as-built record.

-   Missing and wrong circuits. There are no rows for the sander (C4), refiner aux fan (C6), outfeed conveyor or hydraulics pump. C7 is shown as “spare drive feed — terminated, capped”, but it feeds the infeed-conveyor drive (ISO-2043). The blower and dust-extract rows carry legacy “C3-” tags, with their positions not reconciled (note 11). Checklist item 2 (signed 07/12/2026) records the terminations as checked “against the Line 2 Cable Schedule”, yet several installed circuits have no row to check against.

-   Refiner feeder sizing (project plan risk R2, due to be closed out before 07/25/2026). C3-REF-01 and C3-REF-02 are scheduled at 6 mm² for Ib 45 A. MPP-STD-SUM-05 gives Cg 0.80 (drive cubicles grouped in Section C) and Ca 0.87 (45 °C MCC room, 90 °C XLPE), so the required tabulated capacity is 45 / (0.80 × 0.87) = 64.7 A.
    • 6 mm² is 49 A (Iz 34.1 A): it fails.
    • 10 mm² is 66 A (Iz 45.9 A): the minimum on this basis. A larger size is needed if the walk-down finds more than six circuits sharing the run.
    Every other scheduled feeder passes on the same factors at its scheduled size. The removed-cable specification records the pre-upgrade refiner feeder as 10 mm², so the installed size has to be confirmed in the field. If 6 mm² is installed, R2 requires the feeder to be re-cabled before energisation, under its own RFI.

-   Screen termination. Note 2 states both-ends 360° glands, which is what IEC 61800-3 and DTX-IOM-2025-04 §3.2 require. P. Nandwani's notes (07/11/2026) record single-end pigtail bonding, with the motor-end screen left unbonded, on every VFD motor cable terminated: about ten at that date, and the rest to the same method. RFI-025 is open and checklist item 3 is unsigned. The field is corrected to the schedule, not the other way round. The KCC-EMC glands in stores (Rack 09-B, 07/12/2026 extract: 24 × M25, 18 × M32, 8 × M40) cover the job.

-   Construction. Rev B's type column says “4-core … screened/symmetrical”, but its size column says “3c × … + E”. The walk-down records the actual construction against DTX-IOM-2025-04 §3.1, which requires motor cable that is both screened and symmetrical.

Not in the queue

Sander cable re-pull (D. Fenwick, note 08/06/2026). The IR row for IR-L2-SND-04 records “conductors not disturbed”. On the other twelve rows the drive-output conductors were disconnected. The readings also point the same way: phase–earth still rising through the 60 s, and 0.02 MΩ phase–phase. Together they fit a test into the drive output or its FL-C4-01 filter, not a damaged cable.

So the first step is a re-test with the output conductors disconnected, per DTX-IOM-2025-04 §6.1, and DriveTec's view on DR-L2-SND-01 (§6.1, §6.3). A re-pull is raised as an RFI only if the proper re-test fails. If it is, the cable must be screened symmetrical VFD cable with KCC-EMC glands at both ends, and the circuit gets a row on CBL-001. The recovered stock in Rack 12-A must not be used: STK-CBL-0044 and -0045 are unscreened, and IEC 61800-3 does not allow unscreened cable on a drive output.

I've written **Line2_Record_Set_Reconciliation.docx** (saved at `/filesystem/`), with the three sections you asked for. None of the five drawings can go into Simone's pack on its current issue. Four need re-issuing as as-built drawings, checked by 08/14 and issued by Denise on 08/17, so she starts prep on 08/18 with a finished set.

## The calls

|---|---|---|
| Power schematic (PWR-002) Rev C | Re-issue as Rev D | Rev D (Rev C kept only with RFI-014 as the change history) |
| Priya's field markup, 07/09 | Retire it to the change history | Change history only |
| MCC general arrangement (MCC-001) Rev B | Re-issue as Rev C | Rev C |
| Cable schedule (CBL-001) Rev B | Re-issue as Rev C | Rev C |
| Device list (DEV-001) Rev B | Re-issue as Rev C | Rev C |

## Why not present Rev C with RFI-014 and the markup

The standard allows that route, but it can't work here:
- **The markup isn't on a true print of Rev C.** It shows a different incomer and puts the press, sander and conveyor on the wrong MCC sections. It also gives the fuse as "Bussmann-style" rather than the fitted Bramble BFW-80aR, and nobody has checked it.
- **Every drawing leaves out installed equipment, and no RFI covers it.** Eleven drives are installed; the general arrangement and device list show four, the schematic five and the cable schedule six. Simone's Item 2 would fail on the device list alone.
- **Idris's booking asks for the controlled schematic matching the as-built.** A markup doesn't give him that.

## What has to happen before the drawings, all by 08/14
- **Screen bonding (RFI-025):** close it this Monday. The drawings already say 360° bonding at both ends; Priya's notes show screens bonded at one end only, by pigtail. The field gets fixed, not the drawings.
- **Refiner feeder:** on the cable schedule's own figures, 6 mm² fails derating (64.7 A needed against 49 A). Dougie needs to confirm what's actually installed. If it is 6 mm², it gets re-cabled under its own RFI.
- **Vendor RFIs:** Callan has to get DriveTec's answers on RFI-022 (refiner motor cable about 6 m longer than scheduled) and RFI-031 (EMC filter placement).
- **Denise's records:** she has to send the decisions on RFI-017, 021 and 029, and confirm what was issued as MCC-001 "Rev B". Documents dated before 07/08 already cite a Rev B, which suggests the letter was used twice.
